head: byoa docs
text: byoa lets your app run each user's own Claude Code or Codex, on their plan and with their tools, in any sandbox, from inside your own backend. byoa is an open-source library (Apache 2.0). It runs inside your app's own backend. It is not a hosted service. Start with Getting started. To learn the parts first, read Concepts. These pages are the Markdown files in docs/ of the repository. The site at https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs shows the same pages, and serves each page as Markdown for LLMs (add .md to its address) and all of them in llms-full.txt.

head: Start
text: - Getting started: install byoa, make one agents object, serve its two routes, sign a user in and run a first job - Concepts: who brings what, what byoa is and is not, how a job runs, and why real tokens never go into the sandbox

head: Guides
text: - AI login: the sign-in on the lab's own page, where the login stays between jobs, one job step by step, the shared Codex login, and sign-out - Sandbox lifecycle: every sandbox byoa creates, from creation to removal, what each provider does, and what happens when your backend dies - MCP tools and the proxy: connect a user's MCP servers once, the proxy and job tokens, your app's own tools, and calls with a user's grant - Running agents: agents.run and its events, what the agent may do, sandbox modes, jobs at the same time, session and jobToken - Sandbox providers: E2B, Daytona, Instabox and the local sandbox, and how to write an adapter - Stores and Convex: the store adapter, Postgres, Convex, your own database, and a table of its own for the AI logins - Testing: test your app with the fake harness, the local sandbox and the memory store, and run byoa's own tests

head: Reference
text: - API reference: every import, method, option and event - Lab rules: what Anthropic's and OpenAI's terms allow, and what byoa and each app must do - Security: where each secret is kept, and how to report a problem

head: Getting started
text: This page takes you from npm install to a first agent job. Your app's backend makes one agents object, serves two routes, signs a user in to their own plan, and runs a job. A new app needs fewer than 50 lines of its own code for this. The to-do example uses byoa in 35.

head: Install
text: Install byoa from npm. Its package is @madeyexz/byoa, because npm does not allow the name byoa: Also install the sandbox SDK that your app uses: e2b for E2B, @daytona/sdk for Daytona. Instabox and the local sandbox need none. byoa needs Node 22.18 or later, or Bun. To use the newest commit on main before it is released, install from GitHub: npm install github:madeyexz/byoa.

head: Make one agents object
text: Make one agents object in your backend: once for each process, or once in each Convex action. - app: lower-case letters, digits and -, at most 24. It names the app's sandboxes and login volumes. - sandbox: the sandbox provider. To change the provider, change this one line. - store: your own database, through a store adapter. For Postgres, run POSTGRES_SCHEMA once. - encryptionKey: 32 random bytes as base64. Keep it the same between restarts, and keep it secret. - proxyUrl: a public HTTPS URL. The sandbox must reach it. In development, use a tunnel such as cloudflared tunnel --url http://localhost:3000. The default E2B template is named byoa, and a new E2B account does not have it. Build it one time with buildE2BTemplate(), or pass e2b({ template: 'base' }). See Sandbox providers.

head: Serve two routes
text: byoa's handlers are fetch handlers (Request → Response). On Node, wrap your app's handler with toNodeListener from @madeyexz/byoa/node. - The proxy checks the job token itself. Do not put your app's session check in front of it: the harness in the sandbox has no app session. - Every other route reads the user from your app's own session. The userId you give byoa is your app's stable user id. Never take it from a header or a body that the browser controls.

head: Sign the user in to their plan
text: The sign-in runs the unmodified CLI in a sandbox. The user signs in on the lab's own page. byoa gives your app only that page's URL and, for Codex, a code. See AI login for each step.

head: Connect an MCP tool, one time
text: Every later job of this user can have this server. Your app's own data needs no MCP server: give its tools to createAgents as functions. See MCP tools and the proxy.

head: Run a job
text: run does not throw when a job fails. It gives error events, then always one end event. See Running agents for the events, what the agent may do, and jobs at the same time.

head: Let a coding agent do it
text: skills/byoa is a skill in the Agent Skills format. It teaches a coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Amp and others) to add byoa to an app: the install, createAgents with a store and a sandbox adapter, the sign-in, the MCP connections and their routes, agents.run and its events, and the lab rules. To install it in your app's repository: For LLMs, the site also serves the docs as llms.txt (an index) and llms-full.txt (the docs, SPEC.md, the example and the skill in one file), and each docs page as Markdown (add .md to its address).

head: Next
text: - Read Concepts to learn who holds what, and where. - Run the to-do example: an AI-native to-do list, with tests that use the fake harness. - Test your app with no plan and no sandbox: Testing. - Follow the Lab rules. Every app on byoa must.

head: Concepts
text: Your app brings the product. Each user brings the agent. You build the app and pick the sandbox. Each user brings their plan and their tools. byoa runs inside your backend and runs each job in that user's own sandbox.

head: Who brings what
text: Diagram: You build the app and import byoa. Each user signs in with their own plan and connects their tools once. Your app code calls agents.run. byoa is a library inside your app's backend, and keeps AI logins and MCP grants in your database. Below your backend's edge, byoa drives three things that run outside it: a new sandbox for each job at E2B or Daytona on your account, where the user's own Claude Code or Codex runs; the AI labs, whose model calls the user's own plan pays; and the user's MCP servers, which get the real token from byoa's proxy. - You, the developer, build the app, pick the sandbox provider (E2B, Daytona or Instabox, on your own account) and own the database. You import byoa into your app's backend. - The end user uses your app. They have a Claude or ChatGPT plan, and accounts in tools such as Notion or Gmail. They sign in on the lab's own page one time, and connect each MCP tool one time. - byoa is a library in your backend. It keeps the user's AI login and MCP grants in your database, encrypted with your key. For each job, it gets a sandbox at your provider and runs the user's own, unmodified Claude Code or Codex there. - The AI labs (Anthropic, OpenAI) get the model calls. The user's own plan pays for them, not your API bill. - The MCP servers get the real token from byoa's proxy in your backend, never from the sandbox.

head: The problem
text: To make an app AI-native, you run a big lab's harness (Claude Code or Codex) in a sandbox, with the user's own AI plan. For each app, you must build the same connection layer again: - the user's AI login, through the real CLI; - the user's MCP connections and their OAuth tokens, with one refresh owner; - the user's skills and AGENTS.md; - the harness install and its updates; - the code that connects all of this to one sandbox provider. byoa is that layer, as a library, so you do not build it again for each app.

head: What byoa is, and what it is not
text: - byoa is a library. It runs inside your app's own backend (Node, Bun or Convex). Cloudflare Workers support is planned. - byoa stores tokens in your own database, through a store adapter. - byoa is not a hosted service. We do not run a server, and we never see your users' tokens. Version 1 Later --------- Agents Claude Code, Codex Gemini or Antigravity, maybe User plans Claude, ChatGPT Sandboxes E2B, Daytona, Instabox other providers Backends Node, Convex actions Cloudflare Workers Token stores Convex, Postgres, or your own with get, put, delete and compare-and-set

head: How a job runs
text: Your app calls agents.run(userId, task). byoa takes the user's sandbox, loads the user's setup, and runs the user's own harness on the user's own plan. The sandbox lifecycle has every step and every decision. Diagram: One job, from agents.run to the end event 1. Your app calls agents.run. agents.run(userId, { harness, task, mcp, setup }). 2. Take the user's sandbox. By default, resume the user's kept sandbox, or create it for the first job. With sandboxPer 'job', create a new one. 3. Load the setup. The pinned harness, the skills, AGENTS.md, and an MCP config that points to your proxy with a job token. 4. Copy the AI login in. From your database, decrypted in your backend. Login files: login files in. 5. Run the harness. Text, tool calls and permission requests stream back as events. MCP calls go through the proxy. 6. close() This is the end. End the job token, save the login back if the CLI changed it, remove it from the sandbox, then pause or destroy the sandbox. Login files: files removed. The user's AI login and MCP grants stay in your database between jobs. A kept sandbox keeps the files that the app wrote there and the installed harness, but no login.

head: Real tokens never go into the sandbox
text: The agent in the sandbox gets a short-lived job token, for one job and one user. The proxy in your backend adds the real MCP token to each request. Diagram: How an MCP call from the sandbox gets the real token 1. The harness calls an MCP tool. Its MCP config points to your proxy, at <proxyUrl>/<name>, with the job token. It has no real MCP token. 2. Question: Is the job token good for this server? If yes: go on to step 3. - If no: Refuse the call. This is the end. The job ended, or the job did not get this server. 3. Add the real token. From your database, encrypted with your key. byoa refreshes it when it is due, with one refresh owner. 4. Send the request on to the MCP server. This is the end. The answer goes back to the harness. The real token does not. MCP tools and the proxy has the details, and AI login says where the user's AI login is at each step.

head: AI login
text: A user's AI login stays encrypted in your app's database, and is in a sandbox only while a sign-in, a job or a sign-out runs. This page shows how byoa signs a user in to Claude Code and Codex, keeps the CLI's own login files, and uses them for each job. The login tokens are in They are never in ------ the sign-in sandbox, until byoa destroys it what byoa returns to your app your app's database, encrypted the job's environment variables a job's sandbox, only while the job runs a kept sandbox between jobs the state, lease and pending entries in the store This is for the default login, storedLogin(). With cliLogin, the tokens stay in the user's volume instead of the database. byoa never uses the tokens itself and never calls the labs' token endpoints. The unmodified CLI is the only client that sends them to the lab.

head: Sign-in
text: Your app calls agents.connectLogin(user, harness). byoa starts a new sandbox for up to 20 minutes, installs the pinned CLI and runs its own sign-in. The user signs in on the lab's page. byoa gives your app only that page's address and, for Codex, a code. Claude Code Codex --------- The CLI's sign-in claude auth login codex login --device-auth What your app shows a link on claude.com a link on auth.openai.com, and a one-time code What the user does signs in; Anthropic's page shows a code enters the code on OpenAI's page How your app finishes finishLogin(user, 'claude', { code }) with that code; byoa types it into the CLI and waits up to 60 s finishLogin(user, 'codex', { waitMs }), again until the state is no longer pending The files the CLI writes in ~/.claude (CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR): .credentials.json (the tokens) and .claude.json (the account: email, organization, plan) in ~/.codex (CODEX_HOME): auth.json (access token, refresh token, last refresh time) Claude Code also writes a copy of .claude.json in backups/ at each start. byoa removes it and does not store it. Diagram: The sign-in sandbox, from connectLogin to the signed-in state 1. Remove an unfinished earlier sign-in. connectLogin(user, h) destroys this user's earlier sign-in sandbox for the harness, if one waits. Login files: no login files. 2. Create the sign-in sandbox. storedLogin: no volume. cliLogin: the user's volume at ~/.claude or ~/.codex. Time limit: 20 min, then the provider deletes it. 3. Install the pinned CL

head: Where the login stays between jobs
text: In your app's database (the default, storedLogin()) In a volume of the user (cliLogin) --------- How it gets there byoa reads the CLI's files from the sign-in sandbox and encrypts them together with AES-256-GCM, with your encryptionKey or the key you give storedLogin. The entry's name is part of the encryption, so the entry cannot be moved to another user. The sign-in sandbox mounts the user's volume at ~/.claude or ~/.codex, and the CLI writes its files there. Where it is one entry for each user and harness, ailogin/<user>/<harness>, as v1.<iv>.<ciphertext>. It is the only copy between jobs. the volume byoa-<app>-<harness>-<first 24 hex of sha256(user)>, with the files as the CLI wrote them In a job byoa copies the files in and takes them out again (below). Every job sandbox of that user and harness mounts the same volume. byoa never reads or copies the files. The store keeps only the state. Providers all providers with volumes: E2B (when volumes are on for your team) and Daytona, not Instabox To keep the logins in a table of their own, with a key of their own, so that you can give them their own access rules and backups, see Stores and Convex. To use the volume, pass login: cliLogin (from @madeyexz/byoa). The labs' published terms limit where these tokens may be stored. Each app checks them: see Lab rules.

head: One job, step by step
text: This is a job with the default storedLogin(). First byoa checks that the store has the user's login. If it does not, the job stops with LoginError (in run, an error event with code signed-out) and the state becomes signed-out. close() runs steps 4 to 7, also when the job failed. 1. Take the lease. Only one sandbox may hold a user's login at a time, because both CLIs rotate their refresh tokens. byoa writes the lease ailoginlease/<user>/<harness> with compare-and-set. If another job holds it, this job waits up to 10 minutes (storedLogin({ waitMs })), then fails. The lease ends by itself after the job timeout + 5 minutes, so a lost backend does not lock it. 2. Copy the login in. byoa decrypts the entry in your backend and writes the files into the job's sandbox, chmod 600. It remembers which version of the entry it read. CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR or CODEX_HOME points the CLI at them: a folder path, not a token. 3. The CLI runs, and may refresh. The unmodified CLI uses its tokens to reach the lab. When its access token is due, it refreshes it and writes its own files again. 4. Save back what changed. If the files changed, byoa encrypts them and writes them over the entry, only if the entry is still the version from step 2 (compare-and-set). If the user signed in again meanwhile, the newer entry stays. 5. Remove the files. byoa deletes the login files and Claude's backups from the sandbox. If it cannot delete them, it destroys the sandbox instead of keeping it. 6. Give the lease back. Th

head: Codex jobs at the same time: the shared login
text: With login: storedLogin({ parallel: true }), the Codex jobs of one user can run at the same time, each in its own sandbox: a sandboxKey for each job, or sandboxPer: 'job'. Claude Code jobs still run one at a time, because when Claude Code refreshes is not checked yet. Diagram: How a Codex job takes the shared login 1. Question: Will Codex refresh the login before this job could end? Within the lease time, the job timeout + 5 min. If no: go on to step 2. - If yes, or not known: Hold the login alone. The job marks that it waits, so no new job joins. When the sharing jobs end, it takes the lease alone. Codex refreshes, step 4 saves the new login, and the jobs after it share again. Time limit: lease: { alone: { id, until } }, after want. 2. Share the login. This is the end. The job adds itself to the lease's shared list and gets its own copy of the login. More jobs can join. Time limit: lease: { shared: { job1: until, job2: until } }. - To answer the question, byoa reads only the time the access token ends in auth.json, and no token. Codex refreshes 5 minutes before its access token ends, and that token lasts 10 days. When auth.json has no such time, byoa uses 8 days after the last refresh. When byoa cannot tell, the answer is yes. - If two sharing jobs both save a change, the first save wins (step 4). - One risk stays: Codex also refreshes when OpenAI answers 401 to a token that has not run out. If two sandboxes get that answer at the same time, both refresh, one refresh fails,

head: Sign-out
text: agents.signOut(user, harness) deletes the user's kept sandboxes for this harness, signs out with the CLI so that the lab can revoke the login, and deletes the login. Diagram: Sign-out, with the default storedLogin 1. Destroy the user's kept sandboxes for this harness. signOut(user, h) calls deleteSandbox(user, { harness: h }). A job in one of them ends. Login files: no login files. 2. Question: Is a login stored? ailogin/<user>/<h>. If yes: go on to step 3. - If no: Skip the CLI sign-out. Then go on to step 5. 3. Sign out with the CLI in a new sandbox. Takes the login lease alone, writes the files in, and runs claude auth logout or codex logout, so that the lab can revoke the login. If this fails, byoa goes on. Time limit: 5 min; not kept; waits for the lease, max 10 min. Login files: login files in. 4. Destroy it, give the lease back. Login files: no login files. 5. Delete the stored login. The state is 'signed-out'. This is the end. ailogin/<user>/<h> is deleted. With cliLogin, sign-out also destroys an unfinished sign-in sandbox, signs out in a sandbox that mounts the user's volume, and deletes the volume.

head: Sandbox lifecycle
text: This page shows every sandbox byoa creates, from creation to removal, with the default storedLogin(). A sandbox has the user's login files only while a sign-in, a job or a sign-out runs, unless your backend dies during a job. byoa creates three kinds of sandbox: - a sign-in sandbox for each sign-in, which byoa never keeps (AI login shows its steps); - a job sandbox: by default one kept sandbox for each user, harness and sandboxKey, paused between jobs; or, with sandboxPer: 'job', a new one for each job; - a sign-out sandbox, for 5 minutes, where the CLI signs out (AI login).

head: The job sandbox
text: Diagram: A job sandbox, from the start of a job to its end Kept for the user (default): sandboxPer: 'user': byoa keeps one sandbox for each slot, pauses it after a job and resumes it for the next. 1. Pick the user's slot. One for each user, harness and sandboxKey (an empty key when none). usersandbox/<user>/<provider>/<h>/<key>. Login files: no login files. 2. Question: Does another job run in this slot? If no: go on to step 3. - If yes: Wait, then try again. Time limit: max 10 min (waitMs), then an error. 3. Question: Does the slot have a sandbox? If yes: go on to step 4. If no: see "Create a new kept sandbox" below. 4. Resume it. Time limit: job + 1 min. 5. Question: Does the provider still have it? If yes: go on to step 6. - If no: Create a new kept sandbox. Also when it was gone (SandboxGoneError). Time limit: job + 1 min. Then go on to step 6. 6. Empty the work folder. ~/work: nothing of an earlier job stays. 7. Question: Is the user signed in? a stored login exists. If yes: go on to step 8. - If no: Stop with LoginError. This is the end. The state becomes 'signed-out'. close() still runs. 8. Check the MCP servers, install the pinned harness. 9. Copy the login in. Takes the login lease, decrypts the files, writes them, chmod 600. Time limit: waits for the lease, max 10 min; lease: job + 5 min. Login files: login files in. 10. The harness runs. The CLI may refresh its login and write its files again. Login files: login files in. - If backend dies: Warning: If your backend

head: When your backend dies during a job
text: - close() never runs, so byoa does not save the login back or remove the files. - Kept sandbox: the login files stay inside until the next job of the same slot resumes it. The provider pauses or stops it later; on Instabox, it runs until 30 minutes with no activity. See the table below. - If the CLI refreshed its login during that job, the new login is lost. The next job writes the older stored copy over the files. Because both CLIs rotate their refresh tokens, the next refresh may then fail. - New sandbox for each job: the provider deletes the sandbox at job + 1 minute, with the files. - The slot and the login lease end by themselves after job + 5 minutes, so the user's next job does not wait forever.

head: How each provider pauses and times out
text: E2B Daytona Instabox ------------ After a job, a kept sandbox is paused, with no process of the job kept stopped stopped (not Instabox's pause) A kept sandbox whose time ends (your backend died) pauses at job + 1 min stops after job + 1 min with no activity has no time limit; pauses itself after 30 min with no activity (default) A sandbox that is not kept (sign-in, sign-out, new for each job) killed at its time deleted when it stops, at the latest after its time deleted after its time, whatever its state Resume after it paused itself byoa ends any old process first started again; no old process runs byoa resumes, stops and starts it, so no old process runs A paused kept sandbox stays with no time limit until archived, after 7 days stopped with no time limit Volumes for cliLogin yes, when volumes are on for your team one shared volume, a subpath for each login none: use storedLogin()

head: Removal
text: - agents.signOut(user, h) deletes the user's kept sandboxes for that harness, then signs out (AI login). - agents.deleteSandbox(user, { harness?, sandboxKey? }) on its own destroys each matching kept sandbox. A job in it ends. The login and the MCP grants stay. When you delete a user, call agents.deleteSandbox(userId); when you delete a project that had a key, agents.deleteSandbox(userId, { sandboxKey: projectId }). - Nothing else removes a paused kept sandbox.

head: MCP tools and the proxy
text: The user connects each MCP tool one time, and every agent run that your app gives it has it. The real tokens stay in your database. The agent in the sandbox gets only a job token for your proxy.

head: Connect a server, one time for each user
text: - name: lower-case letters, digits and -, at most 32. A job asks for servers by this name. - The URL must be https:// (or http:// on localhost). With bearer, byoa checks the token with one MCP initialize, and throws if the server refuses it. - byoa uses Client ID Metadata Documents when the server supports them (serve agents.clientMetadata() at oauth.clientMetadataUrl), and Dynamic Client Registration only when it does not. - The server's sign-in page sends the browser to your oauth.redirectUrl route, which calls agents.finishMcp({ state, code, error }). It finds the user from the stored state, so that route needs no session. A sign-in that does not finish in 15 minutes runs out; call connectMcp again. - byoa refreshes each grant itself, with one refresh owner: your backend. Two jobs that need a refresh at the same time cause one refresh request. Do not refresh or read the tokens in your app's code.

head: The proxy and job tokens
text: Serve agents.proxy at proxyUrl and at every path below it (<proxyUrl>/<name>). It is a fetch handler. For each job, byoa writes an MCP config in the sandbox that points to the proxy, with a job token for that one job and one user. - The proxy checks the job token, adds the user's real token, and sends the request on to the MCP server. - It refuses a job token after the job ends, and for a server that the job did not get. - Do not put your app's session check in front of it. Each of its answers has the header x-byoa-proxy: 1. - No real MCP token is in the sandbox's environment, files or processes at any time. A test checks this after each job with a real MCP call (V5). A job gets only the servers that your app names in its mcp. A server in mcp that the user has not connected gives an error event with code mcp, and the job runs without it.

head: When the proxy is down
text: Before the harness starts, byoa checks from the job's sandbox that each MCP server of the job answers through agents.proxy. When the sandbox cannot reach the proxy (a wrong proxyUrl, a tunnel that ended, a firewall), the job does not start: run gives an error event with code mcp and ends with ok: false, and session throws ProxyError. A server that does not answer gives an error event with code mcp, and the job runs. Without this check, a harness that cannot reach a server leaves its tools out and still ends well.

head: Your app's own tools
text: Give your app's own tools to createAgents as functions (tools): MCP server name → tool name → { description, input, run }. input is the JSON Schema of the arguments. A job gets them by the server's name in mcp, as it gets a connected server. The harness calls them through agents.proxy, which checks the job token and calls run(args, { user, job }) in your backend, for the user of that job. So you write no MCP server, keep no token for it, and connect nothing for each user. What run returns goes to the agent (a string as it is, other values as JSON); when it throws, the agent gets the message as a failed call. byoa does not check the arguments against input: check them in run.

head: Move a grant into byoa
text: To move an MCP grant that the user already made elsewhere into byoa, call agents.importMcp(userId, { name, url, oauth }) with the MCP SDK's state (client, tokens, at). Delete the old copy, so that the grant keeps one refresh owner.

head: Call a service's other API with the user's grant
text: Some MCP servers have an API next to the MCP endpoint that is not MCP, such as an export. Your backend calls it with the user's grant through agents.fetchWithGrant(userId, 'tasks', 'https://mcp.example.com/export'): byoa adds the current token, refreshed by the one refresh owner, and gives you the response. By default, it sends the token only to the origin of that grant's MCP server. It does not follow redirects, and never gives you the token. When the service's API is on another origin than its MCP server, name that origin in your own configuration, for the MCP server's origin. Only grants of that MCP server can go there, and only to that exact origin: The MCP server, the sandbox and the user cannot add an origin. Each one is an exact origin: https, no path, no wildcard.

head: Running agents
text: Your app runs a job with agents.run. byoa takes the user's sandbox, loads the user's setup, runs the user's own harness on the user's own plan, and streams its events. For a program of your own around the harness, use agents.session; for a harness outside byoa's sandboxes, agents.jobToken.

head: Run a job and stream its events
text: - The events are the same for Claude Code and Codex. The schema is in the API reference. - run does not throw when a job fails. It gives error events (code: signed-out, expired, harness, sandbox or mcp), and always ends with one end event (ok, result, usage). On signed-out or expired, show the sign-in again. - byoa writes skills where each harness reads them (.claude/skills/, .agents/skills/), AGENTS.md (and CLAUDE.md for Claude Code) from one source, and the MCP config in each harness's own format. plugins adds the skills and MCP servers of an Agent Plugins package (readPlugin(readPluginDir(dir))). - byoa installs the pinned version of each harness in each sandbox, so a new pin reaches every user at their next job. - If the client goes away, stop the loop (or call return() on the generator). byoa still ends the job token, takes the login out, and pauses or destroys the sandbox.

head: What the agent may do
text: By default (access: 'full'), the agent has every tool of its harness, with no approval: a shell, file changes and the network. This is for a sandbox that is the job's alone. An app whose agent must only use its MCP tools, such as a to-do list or a mail client, gives the job access: 'read-only': The agent can then call the job's MCP tools and read files, so the harness can still read its skills and AGENTS.md. It cannot change a file or reach the network by itself. byoa only sets each CLI's own options: Codex runs in its own read-only sandbox, and Claude Code gets only its tools that read; each tool it refuses is a permission event. read-only does not hide files: the agent can read each file that its user can read. Use it always with localSandbox() on a user's own computer, where the sandbox isolates nothing.

head: Sandbox modes
text: Where a job runs Jobs of one user and harness at the same time --------- sandboxPer: 'user' (the default) the user's one kept sandbox for that harness, paused between jobs one; another job waits (waitMs, default 10 minutes) a sandboxKey for each job one kept sandbox for each key, such as a project or a conversation, each with its own lease one for each key, but see the AI login below sandboxPer: 'job' a new sandbox, destroyed after the job see the AI login below Sandbox lifecycle shows each step of each mode, and what each provider does.

head: Jobs at the same time
text: With the default stored login, one job of a user and harness holds the AI login at a time, and another job waits for it. So a user's Claude Code or Codex jobs run one after the other in every mode, also with different sandbox keys. Only the fake harness runs them at the same time. For many Codex agents of one user at the same time, each on its own machine, with one sign-in, turn on the shared login and give each agent its own sandbox: (drain is your own function that reads each job's events.) The jobs then share the login while it is not due for a refresh. One risk stays, and Claude Code jobs of one user always run one at a time: see AI login.

head: A program of your own around the harness
text: An app that runs its own program around the unmodified harness (for example its own server, which starts claude or codex itself) opens the job with agents.session instead. It gets the same sandbox, login, pinned harness and job token, and runs its own command: session throws LoginError when the harness is not signed in, and ProxyError when the sandbox cannot reach the proxy.

head: A harness outside byoa's sandboxes
text: A program outside byoa's sandboxes, such as a harness on the user's own computer, gets a job token with no sandbox: const t = await agents.jobToken(userId, { mcp: ['notion'] }) gives t.token and t.mcp (the proxy URLs), with the same rules as a job's token, until t.close(). Send t.token as Authorization: Bearer to each t.mcp[].url.

head: Sandbox providers
text: Each sandbox provider is one adapter with one interface. Version 1 has E2B, Daytona and Instabox, and a local sandbox for development and tests. To change the provider, change the adapter that you give createAgents: e2b(), daytona() and instabox() read their API key from E2B_API_KEY, DAYTONA_API_KEY or INSTABOX_API_KEY when you give none. The sandbox must reach your proxyUrl. Sandbox lifecycle compares how each provider pauses and times out. E2B Daytona Instabox Local --------------- Import @madeyexz/byoa/sandbox/e2b @madeyexz/byoa/sandbox/daytona @madeyexz/byoa/sandbox/instabox @madeyexz/byoa/sandbox/local Package to install e2b @daytona/sdk none none Between jobs, a kept sandbox is paused stopped stopped a folder Volumes for cliLogin yes, when volumes are on for your team one shared volume, a subpath for each login none: use storedLogin() folders Network every public domain Tier 1 and 2: allowed domains only every public domain this computer

head: E2B
text: Use e2b({ apiKey?, template?, timeoutMs? }). It needs the e2b package. - The default template is named byoa, and a new E2B account does not have it: the first job then fails with 404: template 'byoa' not found. Build it one time for each pin change with buildE2BTemplate(), or pass e2b({ template: 'base' }). Any template with Node 20 or later works: byoa then installs the pinned harness in each new sandbox (about 10 seconds). - pause takes a snapshot of the files only where the team can (mode: 'filesystem'), else a full one after it ends the sandbox's processes. E2B keeps a paused sandbox with no time limit. - A kept sandbox that times out (a crash, a lost network) is paused, not killed. When byoa resumes a sandbox that paused itself, it ends any old process first.

head: Daytona
text: Use daytona({ apiKey?, client?, snapshot?, volume?, timeoutMs? }). It needs @daytona/sdk. - pause stops the sandbox, and resume starts it, also from archived (more slowly). A kept sandbox is not ephemeral and has no time to live; Daytona archives it after 7 days stopped. A sandbox for one job is ephemeral: Daytona deletes it when it stops, and at the latest after its time. - Daytona allows 100 volumes for each organization, so with cliLogin the adapter keeps every user's AI login in its own subpath of one shared volume (byoa by default). A sandbox mounts only that user's subpath. - On Daytona Tier 1 and Tier 2, a sandbox can reach only allowed domains, so serve agents.proxy on one of them (for example .convex.site), or use Tier 3 or higher. .workers.dev is on Daytona's list but does not work: a Worker's address has two labels below it (<worker>.<account>.workers.dev), and Daytona does not resolve those.

head: Instabox
text: Use instabox({ apiKey?, apiUrl?, template?, snapshot?, timeoutMs? }). It calls Instabox's HTTP API itself, so it needs no package. - Each sandbox starts from the agent-browser template (Node 22, user user, home /data/home), or from a snapshot that you name (snapshot). - byoa stops the user's sandbox after each job (not Instabox's pause), so the next job starts it again with its files and no process of the last one. A sandbox that paused itself (idle for 30 minutes, or at the plan's longest run) is booted again. A sandbox for one job is deleted after it, and at the latest at its timeoutMs. - byoa gives a sandbox none of your account's Vault items or org Secrets, and leaves its commands out of Instabox's command history, which would otherwise keep their output (and so the AI login that byoa reads back). - Instabox has no volumes, so cliLogin does not work there; the default stored login does. Instabox sandboxes reach every public domain, so a tunnel works for proxyUrl. - On the free plan, a workspace has one sandbox at a time (so one user with one kept sandbox, or one job), three starts a minute (byoa waits when Instabox answers 429), and a run of 2 hours at most before Instabox pauses the sandbox.

head: The local sandbox
text: localSandbox({ root?, volumes?, env? }) is folders on this computer. It isolates nothing: use it only for development and tests, and with access: 'read-only' for a harness on a user's own computer. On macOS, the Codex sign-in works in it; the Claude Code sign-in needs Linux.

head: Write an adapter
text: An adapter implements one interface (src/sandbox/types.ts): create (with volumes), resume, run a command, write a file, pause, destroy, and delete a volume. - keep: true is a sandbox that byoa keeps for the user. When it times out, the provider must pause it instead of deleting it, and no process of that job may run when it resumes. - A provider with no volumes refuses create with volumes. - The API reference has the Sandbox interface.

head: Stores and Convex
text: byoa keeps its state in your own database, through a store adapter: MCP grants, AI logins (by default), login states, sandbox slots and leases. Grants and AI logins are encrypted with your encryptionKey.

head: The store adapter
text: A store is four methods. byoa ships one for Postgres, one for Convex and one in memory for tests. For another database, write your own. The version must change on every write, and a key that is deleted and written again must never get an earlier version back. The one refresh owner of each grant, the login lease and the sandbox slots depend on cas. The to-do example's sqliteStore in examples/todo/todos.ts is one in 19 lines.

head: Convex
text: In a Convex app, byoa's state is one table and four internal functions in your deployment (@madeyexz/byoa/store/convex). Call byoa from actions and HTTP actions, which can make network calls; serve agents.proxy from an HTTP action. A Convex action has a time limit, so set waitMs shorter than the default 10 minutes. On Daytona Tier 1 and 2, .convex.site is an allowed domain for the proxy.

head: A table of its own for the AI logins
text: To keep the logins in a table of their own, with a key of their own, so that you can give them their own access rules and backups: To keep each login in a volume of that user and app instead, behind the sandbox adapter, pass login: cliLogin (from @madeyexz/byoa). Your database then never holds the login. This needs a provider with volumes; see AI login.

head: Tests
text: Use memoryStore() from @madeyexz/byoa. See Testing.

head: Test your app without a plan or a sandbox
text: Use harness: 'fake', localSandbox() from @madeyexz/byoa/sandbox/local and memoryStore() from @madeyexz/byoa. The fake harness runs no model and needs no login. It reads the same MCP config Claude Code would, and calls MCP tools through the real proxy: each task line call <server>.<tool> <json> is one call. So a test proves your app's routes, grants and proxy end to end. - The fake harness shows the task's first line as one text event and skips the other lines. The last call's output is the end event's result. - With the local sandbox, proxyUrl can be http://127.0.0.1:<port>/byoa/mcp. - Copy examples/todo/todo.test.ts. Do not offer fake to end users in production.

head: Test byoa itself
text: - npm test runs V10, V12, the fake-harness tests and the unit tests. npm run test:v11 runs V11; it downloads about 600 MB. CI runs both on every commit. - With DAYTONA_API_KEY set, npm test also checks the Daytona adapter against Daytona (with BYOA_DAYTONA_VOLUMES=1 too, also its volumes; that needs a key with the volume permissions). With E2B_API_KEY too, it runs V4 (test/v4.test.ts), which needs cloudflared to give the proxy a public URL. On a Daytona org on Tier 1 or 2, also set BYOA_V4_RELAY to a relay on an allowed domain, such as test/relay deployed to a temporary Convex project. - npm run test:e2b checks the E2B adapter against E2B and runs V8 there (a user's jobs in one paused and resumed sandbox, and sandboxPer: 'job'). It needs E2B_API_KEY, and with BYOA_E2B_VOLUMES=1 also checks volumes, for an E2B team with volumes turned on. - npm run test:instabox does the same on Instabox. It needs INSTABOX_API_KEY. BYOA_V4_PROVIDERS=e2b,instabox runs V4 on E2B and Instabox. The checks V1 to V16 are in SPEC.md.

head: API reference
text: This page is the agent skill's API reference, skills/byoa/reference/api.md, so a coding agent and you read the same text. This is the API in https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa today (version 0.1, before version 1). It can change before version 1. The source of truth is src/agents.ts, src/index.ts and the files they import.

head: createAgents(options)
text: - oauth.redirectUrl: the app's route that calls finishMcp. - oauth.clientMetadataUrl: an HTTPS URL where the app serves agents.clientMetadata() (a Client ID Metadata Document). Without it, byoa uses only Dynamic Client Registration. - oauth.clientName: the name the MCP server shows on its consent page. Default: app. - sandboxPer: 'user' (the default): the first job of a user and harness creates the user's sandbox; byoa pauses it after each job (E2B pause, Daytona and Instabox stop) and resumes it for the next, with a new job folder. One job of a user and harness at a time. A job's sandboxKey (in run and session) gives the user one kept sandbox, with its own lease, for each key. A sandbox the provider no longer has is replaced by a new one. 'job': a new sandbox for each job, destroyed after it. With the default storedLogin(), one job of a user and harness holds the AI login at a time, so the user's Claude Code or Codex jobs run one after the other in both modes, also with different sandbox keys; storedLogin({ parallel: true }) lets a user's Codex jobs run at the same time. - tools: the app's own tools, as functions in the backend. { todos: { add_todo: { description, input, run } } } is an MCP server todos with one tool. input: the JSON Schema of the arguments (an object schema; default: no arguments). run(args, { user, job }) runs for the user of the job; what it returns goes to the agent (a string as it is, other values as JSON), and what it throws goes to the agent as a fail

head: AI login
text: Method Returns ------ connectLogin(user, 'claude' \ 'codex') { harness, url, code? }. url: the lab's own sign-in page. code: Codex only, the code to enter on OpenAI's page. finishLogin(user, h, { code?, waitMs? }) { state: 'signed-in' \ 'signed-out' \ 'expired' \ 'pending', error? }. Claude: pass code (the code Anthropic's page shows). Codex: no code; waitMs waits that long; call again while pending. loginState(user, h) 'signed-in' \ 'signed-out' \ 'expired' signOut(user, h) void. Also deletes the user's sandbox for h. deleteSandbox(user, { harness?, sandboxKey? }?) void. Deletes the user's kept sandboxes of this app at this provider: all of them (when the app deletes the user), or those of one harness or one sandbox key (when it deletes a project). The login and grants stay. Login drivers: - storedLogin({ store?, encryptionKey?, waitMs?, parallel? }) (default): the CLI's own login files, encrypted in the store. store and encryptionKey default to the app's. One job of a user and harness holds the login at a time, and another waits for it. waitMs: how long a job waits for the login (default 10 minutes). parallel: true: the Codex jobs of one user share the login, each with a copy in its own sandbox, while Codex will not refresh it before the job's time runs out (byoa reads the time the access token ends from the login files: Codex refreshes 5 minutes before it, and its token lasts 10 days). When it is due for a refresh, one job holds it alone: it waits for the other jobs, and t

head: MCP connections
text: Method Returns ------ connectMcp(user, url, { name, bearer? }) { name, connected: true } or { name, connected: false, signInUrl }. Send the browser to signInUrl. finishMcp({ state, code?, error? }) { user, name }. Call it in the oauth.redirectUrl route with the query parameters. listMcp(user) [{ name, url }] removeMcp(user, name) void importMcp(user, { name, url, oauth }) { name }. Moves a grant made elsewhere into byoa; oauth is the MCP SDK's state (client, tokens, at). Delete the old copy, so the grant keeps one refresh owner. fetchWithGrant(user, name, url, init?) Response. A request with the grant's current token, only to the origin of the grant's MCP server (and grantOrigins for it). No redirects. The app never gets the token. clientMetadata() The Client ID Metadata Document to serve at oauth.clientMetadataUrl. name: lower-case letters, digits and -, at most 32. url: https://, or http:// on localhost.

head: The proxy
text: agents.proxy is a fetch handler (Request → Response). Serve it at proxyUrl and every path below it (<proxyUrl>/<name>). It checks the job token, adds the user's real token, and sends the request to the MCP server; for the app's own tools, it calls the tool's run. It refuses a job token after the job ends. Do not put the app's session check in front of it. Each of its answers has the header x-byoa-proxy: 1.

head: run(user, options): AsyncGenerator<AgentEvent>
text: - mcp: names of the user's connected servers and of the app's own tools. - access: 'full': every tool of the harness with no approval (Codex: --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox; Claude Code: --permission-mode bypassPermissions), for a sandbox that is the job's alone. 'read-only': the job's MCP tools, and reading files, so the harness reads its skills and AGENTS.md; no change to a file, and no network but the job's MCP servers. Codex: --sandbox read-only (its shell stays, because it reads a skill with cat; a command cannot write or open a connection), with the job's MCP tools approved in its config.toml. Claude Code: --permission-mode dontAsk with the tools Read, Glob, Grep, Skill and the job's MCP servers; each tool it refuses is a permission event. It does not hide files: the agent can read each file its user can read. - Before the harness starts, byoa sends one MCP initialize from the sandbox to each of the job's servers, through the proxy. When no request reaches the proxy, the job does not start: an error event with code mcp, then end with ok: false. A server that does not answer gives an error event with code mcp, and the job runs. Each run: the user's sandbox (resumed, or created for the first job; with sandboxPer: 'job', a new one), the user's login, the pinned harness, the setup files in a new job folder, the task; then the login is taken out and the sandbox is paused (or destroyed). Stop the loop (or call return()) to end a job early; byoa still cleans up.

head: Events (one schema for both harnesses)
text: run does not throw for job failures: it yields error events and then exactly one end. signed-out / expired: ask the user to sign in again (loginState says the same). mcp: a server is not connected, its grant failed, it did not answer through the proxy, or the sandbox cannot reach the proxy (then the job did not start).

head: session(user, { harness, setup?, plugins?, mcp?, sandboxKey?, access? }): Promise<Session>
text: For an app that runs its own program around the unmodified harness. Throws LoginError when the harness is not signed in, and ProxyError when the sandbox cannot reach the proxy. The app starts the harness itself, so access changes only the files byoa writes (Codex's MCP config). Session: sandbox, work (the job folder with byoa's files), harness, bin (the pinned binary), version, env (login folder, BYOA_JOB_TOKEN, and for Claude Code MCP_TIMEOUT), token, mcp ([{ name, url }] at the proxy), missing (servers not connected), failing ([{ name, message }]: servers that did not answer through the proxy), reportLogin('signed-in' 'expired'), close().

head: jobToken(user, { mcp?, ttlMs? }): Promise<JobToken>
text: A job token with no sandbox, for a harness outside byoa's sandboxes (such as on the user's own computer). { token, job, mcp, missing, close() }. Send token as Authorization: Bearer to each mcp[].url.

head: Store adapter
text: The version must change on every write, and a key that is deleted and written again must never get an earlier version back. The one refresh owner of each grant depends on cas. - Postgres: run POSTGRES_SCHEMA once (or postgresSchema('my_table')), then postgresStore({ query: (sql, args) => pool.query(sql, args) }). - Convex: convex/schema.ts has byoa: convexTable(); convex/byoa.ts has export const { get, put, remove, cas } = convexFunctions(); in an action or HTTP action, store: convexStore(ctx, internal.byoa). Call byoa only from actions and HTTP actions, and serve agents.proxy from an HTTP action. - Tests: memoryStore() from @madeyexz/byoa.

head: The fake harness
text: harness: 'fake' runs no model and needs no login. It reads the same MCP config Claude Code would. Each task line call <server>.<tool> <json arguments> is one MCP call through the real proxy; it shows the task's first line as one text event and skips the other lines. The last call's output is the end event's result. Use it with localSandbox() and memoryStore() (or the app's own store) in tests.

head: Lab rules
text: byoa runs the labs' own CLIs on each user's own plan, so byoa and every app on it follow the labs' published rules. This page has the rules from SPEC.md, and what each app must do.

head: Rules we follow
text: - We run the real, unmodified claude and codex binaries. We never pretend to be another client. A test checks the hash of the installed binaries against the published packages (V11). - The user signs in through Anthropic's or OpenAI's own sign-in page. - One app's AI login is used only by that app. - The labs' terms restrict where an AI login may be stored. byoa keeps it in your database by default, so each app checks those terms and signs its own agreements with the labs.

head: What the labs' terms say
text: byoa follows the labs' published rules as read on 2026-11-22: - Anthropic (legal and compliance) allows an end user to sign in to the unmodified Claude Code binary with their own plan, including where a platform hosts Claude Code. It forbids third parties to "collect, store, or intermediate Claude.ai credentials or session tokens", unless Anthropic agrees otherwise. - OpenAI (Sign in with ChatGPT Terms, effective 2026-11-04) requires that "any persistent storage of Authentication Tokens must be local and under the user's control, not in a remote or managed environment", and that the plan is used "only for the application they connected". Paid or remotely hosted apps must apply to be partners. So byoa MUST: - run only unmodified claude and codex binaries, and never pretend to be another client; - send the user to the lab's own sign-in page; - not share one AI login between apps. The labs' terms above restrict where these tokens may be stored. byoa keeps the AI login in the app's database by default (R1.4), and ships a per-user volume as an option (R1.5). Each app checks the labs' terms for its own use. Each app is responsible for its own agreements with the labs. We plan to sign agreements for our own apps when they have traction.

head: What your app must do
text: Every app on byoa must follow these rules. If a request breaks one, stop and tell the developer. - Run only the unmodified claude and codex binaries that byoa installs (pinned, and checked in byoa's own tests). Do not patch them, wrap them to change what they send, or set headers or a user agent to pretend to be another client. - Send the user to the lab's own sign-in page, from connectLogin. Do not embed, proxy or copy that page, and never ask the user for a password or an API key in place of it. - Never read, export or call the labs' APIs with the user's AI tokens. The CLI is the only client that uses them. Do not call the labs' token endpoints. - One app's AI login is only for that app. Give each app its own app name and its own store. Never share a login between apps. - Real MCP tokens never go into the sandbox. Give a job its servers with mcp: [...]. Never put a grant's token in setup, the task, environment variables or files. - The labs' terms restrict where AI logins may be stored. Anthropic says third parties may not "collect, store, or intermediate Claude.ai credentials or session tokens" without its agreement. OpenAI says stored tokens must be "local and under the user's control", and paid or hosted apps must apply to be partners. byoa's default keeps the login in the app's database; cliLogin keeps it in a per-user volume. Each app checks the terms and makes its own agreements: https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/SPEC.md#lab-rules

head: Security
text: This page is SECURITY.md of the repository. byoa handles your users' AI logins and their MCP tokens. A bug in byoa can give an attacker access to a user's Notion, Gmail or AI plan. Please tell us about each security problem that you find.

head: Report a problem
text: - Do not open a public issue, pull request or discussion. - Use GitHub's private report: go to the Security tab of this repository and click Report a vulnerability. - Tell us what the problem is, how to make it occur, and what an attacker can get. - Do not put a real user's tokens or data in the report. Use test accounts. We will reply within 7 days. We will tell you when we fix the problem, and we will give you credit if you want it.

head: Supported versions
text: We fix security problems in the latest release on npm (@madeyexz/byoa).

head: Where secrets are kept
text: This is how byoa must keep each secret (see SPEC.md). If byoa does not do this, it is a security problem. Secret Where it is Where it must never be --------- The user's Claude or ChatGPT login By default in the app's own database, encrypted with a key that the app gives (R1.4), or as an option in a volume of that one user (R1.5); in a sandbox only while a sign-in, a job or a sign-out runs In a sandbox between jobs, in another app, or with us MCP grants (access and refresh tokens) In the app's own database, encrypted with a key that the app gives (R2.4) In the sandbox (R3.3), in logs, or with us Job token In the sandbox's mcp.json, for one job and one user (R3.1) Valid after the job ends (R3.4) The real MCP token goes only from the app's backend to the MCP server, through the proxy (R3.2). byoa is not a hosted service, so we never get your users' tokens.

head: What we count as a security problem
text: For example: - A real MCP token is in the sandbox's environment, files or processes (V5). - The proxy accepts a job token after its job ends (V6), or for a different user. - byoa keeps a copy of a user's AI login in a sandbox between jobs, stores it without encryption, or one app can use another app's login. - Two refreshes at the same time revoke a grant, or byoa sends a refresh request from a place other than the app's backend (R2.3). - byoa stores a grant without encryption, or writes a token to a log. - byoa runs a claude or codex binary that is not the published one (V11).

head: What is not ours
text: Report these to their owners: - Bugs in a sandbox provider (E2B, Daytona, Instabox), in Claude Code or Codex, or in an MCP server. - Bugs in an app that uses byoa, for example a leaked encryption key or a database that is open to the internet. The app must keep its encryption key secret and keep the proxy in its own backend.
